The Pangas catfish Pangasius pangasius is a large freshwater species whose eggs, measuring approximately 1.3 mm in diameter, produce yolk-sac larvae of a very modest size. Specifically, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], an endotrophic mass that sustains the prolarva through early development. Field surveys indicate that first exogenous feeding typically commences at around 23 days after hatching when water temperatures are held at a stable 28 °C [T = 28 °C], marking the age at birth as nearly one day [ab = nearly one day] in the context of these standard incubation conditions. The duration of this yolk absorption phase is closely tied to the thermal regime, with the 28 °C representing a mid-range value for tropical systems. As the lecithotrophic stage concludes, the mouth-closed larva must rapidly differentiate its visual and feeding apparatus to successfully transition to active prey capture. This early period of endogenous nutrition, though brief, is critical for subsequent growth and survival, setting the stage for the species' remarkably large ultimate body size.

The sexually mature adult of Pangasius pangasius is among the largest of the Pangasiidae, attaining an ultimate total length of up to 300 centimeters [Li = up to 300 centimeters]. This maximum recorded length, derived from extensive field surveys of large river systems, is consistent with the species' position as a bentho-pelagic predator. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, extrapolated from length-weight relationships, reaches approximately 219,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 219,700 grams], a mass that reflects decades of sustained feeding on fish and crustaceans. In contrast, the onset of reproductive activity occurs much earlier in the life cycle. The total length at puberty is recorded at 63 centimeters [Lp = 63 centimeters], a size that a fast-growing individual might achieve within a few years under optimal conditions in productive floodplain habitats. This size threshold triggers gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of gametogenesis, allowing the fish to invest resources into egg production well before approaching its immense maximal dimensions. The disparity between pubertal size and ultimate size underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing early reproduction in a variable environment.

Under optimal thermal conditions, the reproductive physiology of Pangasius pangasius is remarkably productive. At a water temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], gravid females exhibit an exceptionally high maximum reproductive output, producing approximately 800,000 eggs per kilogram of body weight per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 800,000 eggs per kilogram of body weight per spawning event] during the peak of the spawning season. This per-event fecundity, which is derived from a per-kilogram ovary productivity of roughly 800,000 eggs, represents one of the highest recorded values among freshwater teleosts of comparable size. Furthermore, the spawning events themselves occur with considerable frequency; individual females can initiate a new reproductive event approximately 200 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 200 times per year] under captive conditions held constant at 31 °C. This iterative spawning strategy, coupled with the large clutch sizes typical of the species, allows a single female to release millions of fertilised ova over a monsoon season, maximizing recruitment potential in an environment where larval survival is highly variable. Such a high reproductive rate necessitates a substantial allocation of somatic reserves toward gamete production.

The life-history trajectory of Pangasius pangasius is characterized by a protracted growth period following the attainment of sexual maturity. The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 63 cm length threshold, is approximately 2,100 grams [Wwp = approximately 2,100 grams], a critical body mass at which energy is first partitioned toward both somatic growth and vitellogenesis. Reaching this weight ensures the female has sufficient abdominal capacity and lipid stores to support the production of the large, yolk-laden eggs characteristic of the species. Following puberty, the period of juvenile recruitment into the adult population is gradual, with individuals continuing to add substantial mass for many years. The maximum longevity recorded for Pangasius pangasius in natural riverine systems is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] when average water temperatures remain around 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This lifespan, typical of a large-bodied, iteroparous siluriform, enables multiple spawning seasons over the course of a lifetime. The contrast between the rapid early growth to puberty at approximately 2,100 grams and the eventual asymptotic mass of 219,700 grams underscores the species' remarkable capacity for sustained, slow post-maturational growth.

Comparative life-history data across Pangasiidae suggest that Pangasius pangasius occupies an extreme position along the slow-fast continuum, exhibiting both an exceptionally large asymptotic size and a very high fecundity. The ultimate total length of 300 centimeters remains a distinguishing feature even among the largest members of the family. Interestingly, while the species reaches first breeding at a relatively modest size of 63 centimeters total length, it continues to invest heavily in somatic growth for many more years. The documented maximum lifespan of approximately two decades [am = approximately two decades] in a 24 °C [T = 24 °C] thermal regime is consistent with its slow pace of life and absence of semelparous death. The neonates, initially weighing just 0.0012 grams, undergo a phenomenal mass increase of nearly eight orders of magnitude to reach the adult stage. This extraordinary growth trajectory, supported by a per-event fecundity of approximately 800,000 eggs per kilogram of body weight per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 800,000 eggs per kilogram of body weight per spawning event] and about 200 spawning events annually [F_R_i = about 200 spawning events annually], reflects a life-history strategy finely tuned to the productive but unpredictable flood pulse ecosystems of major Asian river basins.
